title: His eating and his voice
source_text: Λέγει δ᾿ ὅτι οὐδὲ τοιαῦτα σιτεῖται σῶμα θεοῦ, ὡς ἔχων αὐτὸν παραστῆσαι ἀπὸ τῶν εὐαγγελικῶν γραμμάτων σιτούμενον, καὶ ποῖα σιτούμενον. ἀλλ᾿ ἔστω, λεγέτω αὐτὸν βεβρωκέναι μετὰ τῶν μαθητῶν τὸ πάσχα, οὐ μόνον εἰπόντα τό· „ἐπιθυμίᾳ ἐπεθύμησα τοῦτο τὸ πάσχα φαγεῖν μεθ᾿ ὑμῶν“ ἀλλὰ καὶ βεβρωκότα, λεγέτω δ᾿ αὐτὸν καὶ διψήσαντα παρὰ τῇ πηγῇ τοῦ Ἰακὼβ πεπωκέναι· τί τοῦτο πρὸς τὰ περὶ τοῦ σώματος αὐτοῦ ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν λεγόμενα; σαφῶς δὲ φαίνεται ἰχθύος μετὰ τὴν ἀνάστασιν βεβρωκώς· κατὰ γὰρ ἡμᾶς σῶμα ἀνείληφεν, ὡς γενόμενος „ἐκ γυναικός.“ ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ σῶμα, φησὶ, θεοῦ χρῆται τοιαύτῃ φωνῇ οὐδὲ τοιᾷδε πειθοῖ. καὶ ταῦτα δ᾿ εὐτελῆ καὶ σφόδρα εὐκαταφρόνητα· λελέξεται γὰρ πρὸς αὐτὸν ὅτι χρῆται ὁ πεπιστευμένος παρ᾿ Ἕλλησιν εἶναι θεὸς ὁ Πύθιος καὶ ὁ Διδυμεὺς τοιᾷδε φωνῇ τῇ τῆς Πυθίας ἢ τῆς ἐν Μιλήτῳ γενομένης προφήτιδος· καὶ οὐ διὰ τοῦτο ἐγκαλεῖται παρ᾿ Ἕλλησιν ὡς οὐ θεὸς ὁ Πύθιος ἢ ὁ Διδυμεὺς ἤ τις ἄλλος τοιοῦτος ἑνὶ τόπῳ ἐγκαθιδρυμένος Ἑλληνικὸς θεός. πολλῷ δὲ τούτου βέλτιον ἦν χρήσασθαι τὸν θεὸν φωνῇ ἐμποιούσῃ διὰ τὸ μετὰ δυνάμεως ἀπαγγέλλεσθαι ἄφατόν τινα πειθὼ τοῖς ἀκούουσιν.
pass_a_gloss: He says that neither does a god's body eat such things (σιτεῖται), as being able (ὡς ἔχων) to present him from the Gospel writings eating, and what sort of things eating. But let it be: let him say he ate (βεβρωκέναι) the Passover (πάσχα) with the disciples, not only having said 'with desire I desired to eat this Passover with you' but also having eaten; let him say he also, having thirsted, drank beside the spring (πηγῇ) of Jacob. What is this to the things said by us about his body? And clearly he appears to have eaten of a fish after the resurrection; for according to us he took up a body, as having become from a woman (ἐκ γυναικός). But neither, he says, does a god's body use such a voice (φωνῇ) nor such persuasion (πειθοῖ). These too are cheap (εὐτελῆ) and very contemptible (εὐκαταφρόνητα); for it will be said to him that the one believed among Greeks to be a god, the Pythian and the Didymaean, uses such a voice, that of the Pythia or of the prophetess (προφήτιδος) who was at Miletus; and not on this account is the Pythian or the Didymaean or some other such Greek god established (ἐγκαθιδρυμένος) in one place accused among Greeks as not a god. Much better than this it was for God to use a voice producing (ἐμποιούσῃ), through being announced with power (μετὰ δυνάμεως), an unspeakable (ἄφατον) persuasion in the hearers.
pass_b_english: He says: “Nor does the body of a god eat such food,” on the ground that he can show from the Gospel writings that Jesus ate, and what kind of food he ate. Well, let it be so: let him say that Jesus ate the Passover with his disciples, not only saying, “I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you” (Luke 22:15), but also eating it; and let him say that Jesus also became thirsty and drank at Jacob's well (John 4:6–7). What has this to do with what we say about his body? And he is plainly shown to have eaten fish after the resurrection (Luke 24:42–43). For according to us he took on a body, as one “born of a woman” (Galatians 4:4).

“But neither,” he says, “does the body of a god use such a voice, or such a way of persuading.” These objections too are trivial and wholly contemptible. For it will be said to him that he whom the Greeks believe to be a god, the Pythian and Didymaean, uses a voice of just this kind, that of the Pythia or of the prophetess who served at Miletus; and yet the Greeks do not on that account charge the Pythian or the Didymaean, or any other Greek god of this kind enshrined in a single place, with not being a god. But it was far better than this for God to use a voice which, because it was proclaimed with power, produced in those who heard it a persuasion beyond words.

choices.choice: 'Jesus' is supplied for the Greek pronoun αὐτόν where needed for clarity; no other addition. The Gospel at John 4:6-7 says Jesus, tired, sat by the spring and asked for a drink; it does not state that he drank, but Origen's πεπωκέναι is translated as he wrote it. Luke 24:42-43: the eating of fish (some manuscripts add honeycomb). Galatians 4:4 γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός. 'The Pythian' and 'the Didymaean' are Apollo of Delphi and Apollo of Didyma near Miletus; the Greek has a singular verb and a singular 'god' (θεός) with both titles, so the English keeps one subject, 'he whom the Greeks believe to be a god, the Pythian and Didymaean'. The name Apollo is not in the text and is not added. 'Proclaimed with power' (μετὰ δυνάμεως) may echo 1 Corinthians 2:4 or 1 Thessalonians 1:5; not cited inline because no wording is quoted. 'Such a way of persuading' renders τοιᾷδε πειθοῖ. Luke 22:15 ἐπιθυμίᾳ ἐπεθύμησα is a Hebrew-style intensive, rendered 'I have eagerly desired'.

'as though he could show' to 'on the ground that he can show' (ὡς ἔχων gives Celsus's ground; Origen goes on to grant the point, so 'as though' wrongly implies doubt)
Luke 22:15 calque 'With desire I have desired' to 'I have eagerly desired'
'He is also plainly shown' to 'And he is plainly shown' (δέ, no καί in the Greek)
Fixed the subject-verb clash 'the Pythian and the Didymaean, believed ... to be a god, use' to one subject with a singular verb, as the Greek has (ὁ πεπιστευμένος ... θεὸς ... χρῆται)
'settled in a single place' to 'enshrined in a single place' (ἐγκαθιδρυμένος)
Tense of the last clause made consistent: 'it was far better ... a voice which ... produced'
Scripture checked: Luke 22:15, John 4:6–7, Luke 24:42–43, Galatians 4:4
